exercises.title: The value that has no negative
exercises.brief: Write negate. The checks include INT_MIN, and one of them asserts something that will look like a typo until you work out why it is not.
exercises.concept: Two's complement has one more negative value than positive, so one input has no representable negation.
hints: There are 2147483648 negative ints and 2147483647 positive ones.

diagnose.prose: Read the check that failed. negate(INT_MIN) cannot be 2147483648, because that value does not exist in an int. Every implementation returns INT_MIN unchanged, and on a machine that traps it would trap instead. This is the one input for which the function has no correct answer.
The toolchain had nothing to say and a check still failed. That is the ordinary case for this class of bug: the arithmetic is legal, the types are right, and one input has no answer.

exercises.after: abs(INT_MIN) is negative for the same reason, on every machine you will use. It is not a bug in your standard library.

exercises.title: A comparison that is not a comparison
exercises.brief: The starter looks obviously true and prints nothing. Compile it with the warnings on and the compiler will tell you what it is really doing.
exercises.concept: When a signed and an unsigned operand of the same rank meet, the signed one converts to unsigned before anything is compared.
hints: What is -1 as a 32-bit unsigned value?

diagnose.prose: The compiler is naming the conversion. a becomes unsigned before the comparison, and -1 as a 32-bit unsigned value is 4294967295, which is not less than 1. The comparison is well defined and it does not mean what it says.
The warning names the rule: two operands of different signedness met, and the signed one converted. Change the types so both sides agree.

exercises.after: -Wsign-compare is enabled by -Wextra. Turn it on and leave it on. Every reverse loop written with an unsigned counter is this bug.

exercises.title: Make the sanitizer speak
exercises.brief: The flags here turn undefined behaviour from silent into loud. Write an add that overflows and watch what the sanitizer says about it.
exercises.concept: -fsanitize=undefined catches the overflow at the moment it happens and names the file and line.

diagnose.prose: Read the runtime error. The sanitizer names the operation, the operands and the type: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int'. That is the whole class made visible.
A check failed rather than the sanitizer firing. Look at which one, and at what your function returns for the ordinary inputs.

exercises.after: -fno-sanitize-recover=all is not optional. Without it the sanitizer prints its complaint and the program still exits 0, so a test suite reports a pass over a program that has already broken its contract.

exercises.title: Two midpoints that disagree
exercises.brief: Both of these compute a midpoint. Both compile cleanly with every warning enabled. They do not agree, and the input that separates them does not overflow anything.
exercises.concept: Nothing complained, and one of them is still wrong for an input you would not have thought to try.
hints: The failing input has a negative operand. What does C do when it divides a negative number?

diagnose.prose: No error, no warning, and a check failed. a + (b - a) / 2 is the form people reach for to avoid overflow, and for mid(2, -1) it gives 1 where (a + b) / 2 gives 0. Integer division truncates toward zero, so (-3) / 2 is -1 and not -2. The divergence has nothing to do with overflow.
Work out both expressions by hand for a = 2, b = -1 before changing anything.

exercises.after: The overflow-safe form is still the right one when the operands can be large. Just know that it is a different function on negative inputs, not the same function written more carefully.

exercises.title: Ask before you add
exercises.brief: Write safe_add so it reports whether the addition was representable, and writes the result only when it was.
exercises.concept: The checked builtins are the honest way to do arithmetic on input you did not choose.
hints: __builtin_add_overflow(a, b, &out) returns true when it overflowed.

diagnose.prose: Read which check failed. The function has to return the opposite of what the builtin returns, and it must still write the result for the cases that fit.
Nothing complained and a check failed. Compare what the builtin returns against what your function returns for the same call.

exercises.after: C23 standardises this family as ckd_add and friends in <stdckdint.h>. Until then the builtin is available in gcc and clang and compiles to one add and one conditional jump.

exercises.title: The loop that never ends
exercises.brief: Count down from n - 1 to 0 and sum the array. The starter uses the type everyone reaches for, and it does not terminate.
exercises.concept: An unsigned counter cannot go below zero, so a test for that never fires.
hints: What is the smallest value a size_t can hold?

diagnose.prose: The loop does not end. i >= 0 is always true for an unsigned type, so when i is 0 the decrement wraps it to the largest size_t instead of going negative, and the loop starts again from the top of the address space.
The loop terminates now but the sum is wrong. Check which elements you visited.
Nothing complained and a check failed. Count the iterations by hand for a three-element array.

exercises.after: Two fixes are idiomatic: loop from n down to 1 and index with i - 1, or use a signed counter. The first is preferred because it keeps the index type matching the container's.

exercises.title: Widening is an instruction
exercises.brief: load reads one byte and returns it as an int. The checks include a byte whose top bit is set, and the answer depends on a single character in the declaration.
exercises.concept: Whether the high bits are copies of the sign bit or zeros is decided by the type, and it becomes a different instruction.
hints: 0xFF as a signed char is -1. As an unsigned char it is 255.

diagnose.prose: The failing check uses a byte with its top bit set. Plain char is signed on this target, so the value sign-extends and you get a negative number where the check wants 255. The compiler emits movsx for one and movzx for the other.
Nothing complained and a check failed. The types are all legal; only one of them means what the checks expect.

exercises.after: This is why char is the wrong type for a byte. Use unsigned char for data and char only for text.

exercises.title: Say what you mean instead
exercises.brief: Rewrite the overflow check so it asks a question the standard answers. The starter tests the result of an operation the standard says does not happen.
exercises.concept: Check the operands before the operation, not the result after it.
hints: a + b overflows exactly when b > INT_MAX - a, and that comparison is well defined.

diagnose.prose: The check that failed passes two large positive values. a + b < 0 asks about a value the standard says cannot exist, so the compiler is entitled to conclude the test is never true and delete it. Ask about the operands instead.
Nothing complained and a check failed. The test you wrote is legal C and the compiler removed it, which is why nothing was reported.

exercises.after: Both operands need a guard: positive overflow when b > INT_MAX - a, and negative when b < INT_MIN - a.
